claim: Art students who explored objects at length and kept the problem open produced work rated more original (r=.54 between discovery concern at the formulation stage and originality, in one secondary report). Only secondary sources were read; no primary coefficients, no direct replication.
agent_test: Open-mode arm: force an exploration phase before commitment vs commit-first, rate originality blind, equal tokens.

claim: Conceptual replications in other domains and ages (adolescent writers N=16; 11 Grade 11 art students with 196 portfolio events) point the same way: more exploration goes with more original products. Samples are tiny.
agent_test: Count exploration moves before the first commitment in agent traces and correlate with blind originality.

claim: Originality varies mostly within a person between situations (89% of variance at event level, student level not significant), so exploration is an act that can be prompted, not only a trait.
agent_test: Test that a prompted exploration step lifts originality for the same model across tasks.

claim: Meta-analysis (40 studies, 6,649 participants, 196 effects): problem finding correlates with creativity at random-effects r=.22 (CI .11 to .32), I2=98.7%; dropping one r=.99 outlier gives .196; Egger intercept significant. A modest, very heterogeneous association. Source is one dissertation.
agent_test: Use r about .2 as the prior: do not expect large lifts from a problem-finding step.

claim: Problem finding is not the same as divergent thinking: links are mixed or negative for quality, strongest for verbal flexibility (r=.71-.76, N=90 sixth graders) and weak for figural tasks. In the meta-analysis the fluency moderator CI (-.08 to .63) includes zero.
agent_test: Measure flexibility (number of distinct frames) separately from count of ideas when scoring reframes.

claim: A real-world problem-finding task predicted creative accomplishments better than divergent-thinking tasks (N=77 children); coefficients not seen.
agent_test: Score agent reframes against downstream solution quality, not against idea count.

claim: Problem construction ability predicts solution originality and quality in humans, with a cue-consistency boundary: benefit appears when problem cues are inconsistent (N=195, 6 problems).
agent_test: Run reframing only when the prompt contains conflicting cues; skip it when cues agree (gating test).

claim: Telling teams to restate the problem first gave a marginal originality gain (F(1,63)=2.06, reported p=.078, eta2=.03; the p matches a one-tailed test, two-tailed would be about .16), no quality gain, but less conflict and more satisfaction. Treat as null on outcome.
agent_test: Test restate-first as a cheap control; expect no quality gain at equal tokens.

claim: Restating a problem in more distinct ways predicts both more original (beta=.41) and more harmful (beta=.29) ideas (N=155): reframing amplifies both, so it needs a safety check. No agent harm rate for benign reframing exists; the nearest measured effect is that reframing a request as verse raised attack success from 8.08% to 43.07% (d15).
agent_test: Pair every reframe with a constraint and harm check; measure harm rate with and without reframing.

claim: In the largest controlled LLM reframing test (N=280 after exclusions, 15 expert raters) GPT-4o did not raise novelty or usefulness of problem frames in any mode; experts gained 12.54% more novel frames than novices (p=.01), so the LLM widened the skill gap. SCHEMA keeps O8 as [S].
agent_test: Replicate with an agent that has a reframing operator vs none at equal tokens, split by prompt skill level.

claim: A structured reframing prompt (Dorst frames) was picked as interesting more often (29/189 vs 17/189) in a seven-student study; tastes varied. It does not contradict the null above because the outcome (interest) differs from rated novelty.
agent_test: Compare structured vs free reframing templates on blind interest and novelty ratings.

claim: LLM judges overrate model-written research questions relative to the questions authors actually asked (novelty mirage); expert checks did not agree with LLM judges.
agent_test: Never grade the agent's own reframes with the same model; use a held-out judge or expert.

claim: LLM ideas are rated more novel than expert human ideas: per review means 4.84 (human) / 5.64 (LLM) / 5.81 (LLM reranked by humans) over 109 reviews each; per idea 4.86 / 5.62 / 5.78 over 49 ideas each. Judge agreement with humans was weak. Do not mix the per-review and per-idea figures.
agent_test: Dedupe generated frames before scoring; track unique frames per token, not raw count.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Models fail to notice missing information: QuestBench models score over 80% picking the question in math but 40-50% or lower on logic and planning; they say not sure on 0.7-4.6% of Planning-Q where 41.8% are underspecified.
agent_test: Add a check that asks what is missing before solving; measure abstain and ask rate on underspecified items.

claim: Models can label a question ambiguous when asked but almost never ask in normal answering (answer rate above 95%); GPT-4 proposes solutions to unsolvable MacGyver problems; reasoning models spend more tokens on missing-premise questions and rarely abstain. Several independent benchmarks agree.
agent_test: Test a forced pass asking whether anything is missing or unsolvable, at equal tokens, on MiP, MacGyver and QuestBench items.

claim: A separate detection step for missing information raises agent performance: SWE-bench Verified with hidden info, Claude Sonnet 4.5 54.8% (hidden) to 61.2% (single prompt) to 69.4% (separate detector), equal to prompted interactive 70.4% (p=.62). Another model's interactive baseline fell to 47.2% from instruction failure. Partial non-code and cost evidence added: see K29 and K30.
agent_test: Replicate split detector vs single prompt at equal tokens on a non-code benchmark.

claim: Scaffolds that choose questions by explicit information gain beat model-only questioning (Battleship targeting F1 0.367 to 0.764 for Llama-4-Scout; 0.450 to 0.782 GPT-4o). Authors of the 2025 paper not verified. Opened later (d07, d08): exact EIG needs an enumerable space (Battleship boards); for open spaces the method samples the model's own candidate solutions and splits them, which beat model-only question choice but with a gap that shrinks for stronger models.
agent_test: Use a program-side scorer for candidate clarifying questions where the hypothesis space can be enumerated.

claim: Listing what information is missing and then verifying it beats a direct is-this-enough judgement (explanation alignment 4.02 vs 3.89 out of 5; FaithEval gain over 15% after reconfiguration).
agent_test: Test identify-then-verify vs a one-shot sufficiency check.

claim: Step-back abstraction helps science and knowledge tasks (PaLM-2L MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2) but gives no gain on GSM8K (84.3 vs 84) and breaks some correct answers (11.9% new errors on Physics). A reframe operator is positive on knowledge tasks, null on arithmetic.
agent_test: Gate abstraction by task type; compare fixed vs broken answers.

claim: Having the model rewrite the question before answering lifted GPT-4 from 64.95 to 89.77 average over ten tasks; gains were large where the question was oddly worded, small on clean multiple choice (CSQA 84.09 to 85.45). Stronger models gain more.
agent_test: Run rephrase-then-answer at equal tokens vs plain answer and vs best-of-2.

claim: Self-reflection and divergent-then-convergent prompting modestly help on creative tool problems (infeasible answers down 9.7% with self-reflection, efficient answers up 6.5% with div-conv) in GPT-4 on 180 problems.
agent_test: Reuse as a cheap baseline arm.

claim: GPT-3 analogy prompts were rated helpful and changed how the problem was stated in about 80% of cases, but up to 25% of outputs were potentially harmful and one example beat zero or three. Ratings only; no outcome test.
agent_test: Check the effect of example count when asking for analogy-based reframes.

claim: No study was found that scores an LLM on the classic Getzels paradigm (open problem, exploration before commitment, expert rating). The only replication of the design found is Moore (1985) with writers (N=16, group comparison), not the original still-life experiment.
agent_test: Build the paradigm as a benchmark: open task, count exploration steps, blind ratings.

claim: Reported long-term follow-up claims (problem finders more likely to remain artists) conflict across secondary sources on timing and counts (5, 6, 7, 11, 18 years; 27 of 31 vs 31 of 31 found). Not read in a primary source.
agent_test: None; do not cite exact follow-up numbers.

claim: Theory models that structure problem finding (Getzels presented vs discovered; Dillon recognition, discovery, invention; Abdulla and Cramond five-level hierarchy; Mumford construction) are untested as agent designs; the label used did not change meta-analytic results.
agent_test: Map hierarchy levels to S1 sub-steps and check whether stepwise use beats a single reframe call.

claim: Systems that mine anomalies or build problem-solution trees to find new problems report gains only on weak measures (unique ideas 3.4x; cosine similarity). A research-question certificate scored 4.86 vs 4.38 on 10 topics by LLM rescore. All thin and unreplicated.
agent_test: Treat as hypotheses; test certificate fields vs a plain reframe with blind ratings.

claim: Moore (1985) replicated the Getzels design with 16 middle school writers: the creative group scored 16.3 vs 3.0 on the formulation total, and essays were rated more original; process total vs originality r=.58. Two judge groups agreed r=.92 on originality. Group comparison, small N, not peer reviewed.
agent_test: Log the same process features (options handled, rarity, mid-task reframes) in an agent open-mode phase and check they predict blind originality ratings.

claim: The coefficients of the 1976 study are known only second-hand and differ by source: r=.65 (N=31) for the process total vs originality and r=.42 for unusualness (via Moore); r=.54 for concern for discovery vs originality (via Abdulla for the 1971 paper). Scoring recipe: objects handled, rarity of objects chosen, arrangement, openness over time, changes of structure, interview rating 1 to 5. The primary book and 1971 paper were not opened (gap 5 half closed).
agent_test: Do not cite a single Getzels r; use 'moderate positive, about .4 to .65, N=31'.

claim: Across code and non-code tasks, a structured ask-or-answer decision beats a plain prompt at equal pass count: ClarifyAgent (4 modules, 5 passes) 88.0 vs 57.9 average accuracy (Qwen-2.5-7B) and 88.4 vs 71.2 (Llama-3.1-8B) on ClarifyMT-Bench; models answer too early and decline with each turn. On code, hidden requirements cost 7.8 to 19.8 pass@1 points. The structure costs accuracy where the user already gave the detail (Qwen P 96.6 to 85.3).
agent_test: Test an S1 detector on a non-code open task at equal tokens, scoring both missed gaps and unneeded questions.

claim: Carrying an extra missing-information check in the same prompt costs task success: average 28.6% to 27.8% to 27.0% over five agent benchmarks and five backbones, with drops of up to 13 points on hard tasks (REAL 32.1% to 19.2%) and none on ALFWorld (57.5% to 58.9%). Single-author preprint; mechanism (shared reasoning budget) is the author's reading.
agent_test: Run the S1 check as a separate cheap call or only on a trigger, and report success on well-specified items.

claim: An early-exit rule that watches a reasoning trace for uncertainty keywords stopped 47 to 75% of ill-posed items at 1 to 6% false stops on well-posed items and saved 38 to 70% of tokens on ill-posed items (12 reasoning models); generic entropy-based early exit saves 12 to 22% on math. No study turns the stop into a clarifying question and measures final answer quality.
agent_test: Add a trace monitor that, on trigger, stops and asks one question; compare tokens and final correctness against letting the model finish.

claim: Information-gain scoring of questions works without an enumerable hypothesis space if the agent samples its own candidate solutions and picks the question that splits them best (20-questions with free guesses; 48 code tasks), but the advantage shrinks for stronger models and it adds LLM calls. Exact EIG is only available when hypotheses can be enumerated (Battleship; human mean 1.27 bits, k=1 LLM 0.65 bits, k=5 matches human average).
agent_test: Compare sample-then-split questions with one best-guess question at matched tokens on open design problems.

claim: A forced explore-first prompt (brainstorm without the task constraints, then pick one and build) gave about 1.6 times more distinct high-utility tasks than a plain or step-by-step prompt (12 vs 8 at K=50) and won 96.67% of 20 blind novelty pairs by three experts. One model, one domain, tokens not matched.
agent_test: Equal-token test of explore-first vs commit-first on open agent tasks with blind human ratings (gap 1 still open).

claim: LLM judges are poor stand-ins for human creativity ratings even from another model family: Kendall tau between a Llama-3.3-70B judge and humans on human-written stories was .31 for elaboration, .23 for creativity, .17 for novelty and about 0 for surprise, and the judge gave perfect scores to most AI stories; automatic metrics correlated at or below .29. Execution-gated distinct-output counts (effective semantic diversity) are a possible cheap proxy but are not validated against human ratings of reframes.
agent_test: Validate dedupe-count-with-quality-gate against human ranks on a small set of reframing tasks before using it as the metric.

claim: Reformulation helps when the surface form is the obstacle and not otherwise: rewording failed math questions into familiar structures recovered up to 15.5% accuracy (largest for weaker models and varied phrasing; no resample control), while logically nontrivial rewrites cut consistency (contrapositive 72.4% in one search summary, not opened).
agent_test: Gate O8 on a trigger (low confidence, weak model, varied phrasing) and keep an equivalence check on the reframed problem.

claim: The age pattern in the meta-analysis (children .297 from 47 effects, adolescents .113 from 26, adults .207 from 123) is confounded with domain (age and domain explain variance together, no significant interaction) and rests on nested effects; independent studies per cell are unknown. Treat it as unexplained noise, not a finding.
agent_test: Do not use age to set any agent rule.

claim: No measured harm or constraint-violation rate exists for benign reframing in agents. Closest: restating the same harmful request as verse lifted attack success from 8.08% to 43.07% on 1,200 prompts (25 models), and recasting requests as tool calls cut refusals by 10.9 to 40.2 points (ICML abstract, not opened).
agent_test: Count constraint violations and unsafe content on benign tasks with and without O8, with a non-LLM check where possible (gap 6 open).
